images.caption: The Statue of a young man wearing a chlamys is a Ancient Roman sculpture from the early 1st century that represents a naked boy wearing a chlamys. The work was discovered in 1946 on Calle de la Caridad in Cartagena (Spain) by the archaeologist Antonio Beltrán Martínez and initially identified as Mercury, although it was later described as the imitatio of a previous statue whose prototype, from the 5th century BC, would come close to the conception of the Dresdner Knabe.

images.caption:
Mosaic mural in Parque de Alfonso Torres of Cartagena (Spain), work of the painter Enrique Gabriel Navarro in 1972.
In the mural a woman is seen holding before Carthago Nova the two mural crowns that were awarded by Scipio Africanus for the taking of the city in the Second Punic War, and a fragment of the the Poem of Scipio is quoted in the lower left:

"It was just, because if to Rome, as a codex tells, every assaulted city cost a crown, Cartagena was a force that cost two!"

images.caption: Rear view of the site of the former Casa Llagostera (Cartagena, Spain), in a photograph taken from Plaza del Rey. The Art Nouveau facade of the building, facing Calle Mayor and protected for its heritage value, has been preserved and is supported by scaffolding following the demolition of the structure in 2010. Redevelopment works are currently suspended following the discovery in 2016 of remains of the Ancient Roman harbour of Carthago Nova, and the plot is covered with abundant vegetation.
